title: Habit Strength, Medication Adherence, and Habit-Based Mobile Health Interventions Across Chronic Medical Conditions: Systematic Review
abstract: Unintentional medication nonadherence is common and has been associated with poor health outcomes with increased health care costs. Previous research examined habit’s direct effect on adherence and interactions with factors that influence or overrule it. However, the relationship between habit and adherence, and the role of habit-based mobile health (mHealth) interventions, remains unclear. This review aimed to systematically evaluate the most recent evidence for habit strength, medication adherence, and habit-based mHealth interventions across chronic medical conditions. A keyword search was performed on the PubMed database, and abstract and full-text screening was conducted. PRISMA guidelines were followed when reporting evidence. Of the 687 records examined, 11 met the predefined inclusion criteria and were finalized for data extraction, grading, and synthesis. Most included studies were cross-sectional, used a theoretical model, and measured habit strength using the self-report habit index and self-report behavioral automaticity index. Habit strength was positively correlated with medication adherence in most studies. Habit mediated the effects of self-efficacy on medication adherence, and social norms moderated the effects of habit strength on medication adherence. Habit strength also moderated the effects of poor mental health symptoms and medication adherence. None of the included studies used or proposed a habit-based mHealth behavioral intervention to promote medication adherence. Overall, stronger habit was associated with higher medication adherence, regardless of theoretical model and/or guiding framework. Habit-based interventions should be used to increase medication adherence, and these interventions could leverage widely available mobile technology tools, such as mobile apps or text messaging, and/or existing routines.
